p: Yes.
Do people do that?

People do. So there's a phone number on every ambulance bill

for our billing vendors call center, and they can call and talk through the options there. But there is a charity care program that's based on the same household size and income guidelines that Health and Hospitals uses.
Okay. All right. And then response time for ambulances. What is it generally? Up, down, in between? How does— how is it going? And I appreciate your support for parity strongly.

And we should— we appreciate your support as well. And just to your training comment, you know, I've met with many of you and we've talked about strategies on how to get messaging out, because the real success is not having a fire to begin with. The real success is not going into cardiac arrest from the beginning. So when we prevent those things, that's where the real life-saving work is. So, I appreciate all of you spending time with me talking about different ways to get your constituency, you know, on message as to what they can do to keep themselves safe. Response times, as we've seen, they can fluctuate, but we have

seen that response times are going up. And this is quite honestly why I'm coming out so loudly for EMS parity. When we have an increase year after year in demand for 911 services and we have staffing that is going in the other direction due to recruitment and retention challenges, that equation will lead to increased response times. Now, there are other things that cause increased response times too. That's not the only thing that we can point to. There are things like– I know when I started, there were 20 additional hospitals within the five boroughs than there are right now. So as hospitals close or, you know, our EMTs, our paramedics need to go further, they need to wait longer in the emergency rooms that need to absorb that additional call volume. You know, there are lots of different things that go into this problem, things that we are taking very seriously. And any possible solutions that we can come up with to reduce response times, including, as Chief Miano was talking about a minute ago, you know, moving units into areas of higher demand, and we watch the demand across the five boroughs all day, every day. So we see where there are areas that are really

getting inundated with calls, or response times are higher, and we're able to shift some, but that doesn't mean that response times automatically go down altogether, right? So it may go down in that area, and we'll have to shift some resources around. But it is something that we watch very closely. Because the– you know, there are so many different factors that go into it.
Thank you. Maybe second round, I want to ask about rumbler sirens versus loud sirens. Thank you.
So do you have a preference? I— there are some people that really like the rumblers.
Yes, I like the rumblers. I live in between St. Luke's and Roosevelt.
Yeah.

And it's all day and all night. And so I have complaints all day and all night. So I'm just wondering that when I talk to the union, they like the loud sound. But I think we should think about sirens. I mean, I feel like bringing them all to City Hall Park and just blasting

them all day long, because then somebody might do something about it. I have bills to do it, but I could use some help in thinking about sirens because it– you know, we got a quality of life issue that is– if you don't live near a hospital, you don't hear it. I got two hospitals right next– in the middle.
Understood. Yeah.
So, I would love siren discussion.
We would love to have siren discussion.
Thank you.
Okay. Thank you, Council Member Banks. And then we're going to go back Chair Ariola.

Thank you, Chair, and to the Commissioner, thank you for coming today. One of the concerns I frequently hear from residents in my district, particularly those living in the southern portion of the district, is the perception that the fire and EMS resources are located too far away from where they live. And I want to know, how

does the FDNY evaluate potential coverage gaps and determine whether a neighborhood is being adequately served, and what role do community feedback, call volume, response times, and pollution growth play in that analysis?
There are definitely some areas in the city that have stations that are further away. EMS stations we're talking about, right?
Right.

But with the— with the call volume that we're experiencing, those stations aren't really having a significant impact on where they are because our ambulances are out serving the public 24 hours, seven days a week. So what generally happens is when an ambulance has a run and they take that person to the hospital, they become available.
Right.
So they automatically now become available for the area that they're in as the closest resource. So, uh—
And what about fire trucks or firehouses?
So, firehouses are more distributed across the–
[interposing] Right.
the city. There are far more firehouses than there are EMS stations. EMS stations, I think we have about 40 EMS stations–
[interposing] Right.
and over 200 firehouses. So, there tend to be a more equal distribution of firehouses than there are

Right. Particularly— let me go to some other questions. When it comes to NYCHA emergency response challenges, there was a recent study done by the Elevator Advocates, and this was relegated particularly— well, particularly dealing with the 42nd Council District, which stated that there were close to five buildings in my district which had chronic elevator outages. So I want to know particularly with these elevator

outages that have taken place, has that been a barrier, or has that played in the response time, particularly when it comes to NYCHA developments?
So the Fire Department, we have an elevator task force, and we work closely with NYCHA and the NYCHA elevator team.
Right.

So, we have a pilot program that we've expanded that when the Fire Department receives a call for a defective elevator or somebody stuck in an elevator, at the same time, we will also notify the NYCHA elevator team, and at times, we could have an elevator mechanic meet us at the scene and resolve that problem sooner.

What about just general response times to someone who may be calling for calling 911 for some type of help. What is— what is the– has that been a barrier? Has there been situations where there's been an elevator outage that has blocked or prevented access to that particular call?
So, you're asking about emergency operations in a building when there's an elevator out of service.
Correct.
That's entirely something that can happen and does on occasion.
Right.
I don't have the specific stats on that.

So that goes to my broader point on response time, particularly when it comes to NYCHA residents, or residents when we– it's been reported in my district that we have five buildings that have chronic elevator outages. And I just want to hone in on what's being done as far as any— is there any coordination with NYCHA and with some of these private developers that are now managing these developments?

So, specifically with NYCHA, we do have coordination about the elevators. We report when we operate there and have an elevator out of service, we do report that to NYCHA, and it becomes their responsibility to repair it.
So, has the FDNY observed situations where elevator outages have created barrier delays of responding to emergencies within NYCHA, to be more specific?
Yes, that happens occasionally, but I don't have the stats for how many.

And if so, what coordination exists between the FDNY and NYCHA to address these challenges to ensure that residents can receive timely emergency assistance, particularly seniors or individuals with disabilities and residents living on the upper floors?
We would notify NYCHA when we discover an out-of-service service elevator.
And when it's not per se NYCHA, and what's the coordination when it comes to a RAD/PACT converted development?
We would deal with the managing agent then.

Okay. Has the FDNY identified any developments that consistently present operational challenges due to chronic elevator

outages? And if so, are there any proactive measures being taken to mitigate those risks Before the emergency occurs?
In those— in those new complexes or with the new managing agents, we have not identified that at this time.
Thank you, Madam Chair.
Chair Ariola?

Thank you. I'd like to discuss the fifth firefighter, and the deployment of the fifth firefighter on engine companies has long been a priority for labor and a point of ongoing discussion between the council and the administration. The operational case is straightforward. More personnel on scene means faster knockdown times, fewer injuries, and better outcomes for New Yorkers. So what does the data show about the fifth firefighter's effects on fire suppression outcomes, including time to knock down a fire, firefighter injuries and civilian casualties?

Thank you for that question. The— we do not have specific data that

shows the difference of operations with four firefighter engines and five firefighter engines, right? When we break down our fire reports that talk about civilian injuries and firefighter injuries, we don't have the ability to differentiate between the two. While we certainly welcome additional resources, the ability to stretch and operate hose lines is increased and better and more effective with five firefighters than with four.

Okay, so would it be safe to say that if a fire is– a fire happens and the first due arrives and they have only four members on that rig and that fire is out of control, the— they have to wait for the next second due to come, which would have the fifth firefighter on it before they get water on a fire. Is that correct to say?
The 5th firefighter speeds up the the stretching of the hose lines, and putting water on the fire.
But water doesn't get on that fire until that second rig arrives. Is that true?
Not necessarily, but it’s–
Now, now, is it true?
No, not— if that first engine stretches the hose line and they're ready to operate, they're going to operate. It happens faster with the fifth firefighter.
Right, so if it happens faster, what does that mean? Does that mean that the fire doesn't spread more quickly?
We would theoretically put the fire out quicker. Yes.
It would mean that lives would be in less danger.
Yes, we would put the fire out quicker.

Okay. All right, good. So I think that's a pretty good analysis. So have you conducted any internal analysis or pilot of the fifth firefighter deployment? And if so, what were the results internally? Have you— discussed?

We don't have any formal studies done with it, but anecdotally it would lead

to quicker hose line stretches and quicker extinguishment of the fire.
Thank you. And what is the current average response time by borough, and does the data show meaningful disparities between boroughs that a targeted fifth firefighter deployment could address?

So we do have the average response time to structural fires so far this year. For Manhattan, four minutes 39 seconds. Bronx, four minutes 58 seconds. Brooklyn, four minutes 10 seconds. Queens, five minutes two seconds. And Staten Island, five minutes five seconds. And what was the second part of that question?
It was, what is the current average response time per borough, and does the data show meaningful disparity between boroughs that a targeted fifth firefighter deployment could address?

That's one of the– I will point to the discussion about the fifth firefighter. We don't know– we don't know what impact it would have on response times, because it's putting another

firefighter on the seat of an engine that's already responding. But it does put water on a fire sooner if the first responding rig has a fifth firefighter, correct?
Correct. But that–
[interposing] Right.
apparatus would theoretically arrive at the same time.
Correct. So the more apparatuses that have a fifth firefighter on it, the quicker water gets on a fire, and the ability to cause that fire to not spread reduces, and lives can be saved.
I would agree with that.
Okay. Geographical need— is there a targeted deployment? I think you just gave us kind of what they were— the percentage were per borough.
The discussion about the fifth firefighter is in the Bronx, is in engine companies in the Bronx.
Okay, and can you provide a breakdown of fire incidences by borough and by engine company over the past three fiscal years?

Yes, I have for all engine companies throughout the city, we have the breakdown for fiscal years 23, 24, and 25 of the number of structural and non-structural fires they've responded to. And, you know, as you can imagine, it's not evenly distributed. We have some very, very busy companies and we have some not so busy companies. Right. So this— so right now the fifth firefighter is in what areas?

So we have currently– we have 20 engine companies that have five firefighters, and that is distributed throughout the city in areas that have the types of buildings that generally require longer hose line stretches. So–
[interposing] Okay, so what are the specific concentrated areas right now?

Well, they're not— with the fifth firefighter, they're spread throughout the

city. Every borough has some engines with five firefighters.

So do you think that the fifth firefighter should be in concentrated areas? Do you think it works better? Does that model work better than having them sporadically placed unevenly throughout the boroughs?
But they're placed in areas where their building stock requires those longer hose line stretches.

Okay, so let's just talk about it. The Bronx consistently has among the highest rates of structural fires and fire-related fatalities in the city. Does the FDNY's internal data support a targeted fifth firefighter deployment in high incident boroughs like the Bronx and, secondly, Queens, as you mentioned?

We would certainly welcome any additional resources, and it could have an impact on putting out those fires quicker. But, you know, the fires that we're seeing in the Bronx, putting them out quicker is— or the fifth firefighter is only not necessarily a silver bullet to stop— to

solve all of those problems, right? Stopping and preventing the fire in the first place, sharing the message about closing the door so that the fire doesn't spread before we get there. It's a comprehensive approach to deal with this fire problem. And isn't the fifth firefighter very, very important, especially in vertical fires, in getting the hose up and buildings and more and more into the outer boroughs, not just Manhattan or in the Bronx, but in the outer boroughs we're having more and more vertical buildings that are being built. Doesn't that help in putting fires out?
The taller the building, the longer the hose line stretch.
Correct.
The more impactful the fifth firefighter.

The more we build and the more we have, you know, we have larger buildings in areas that didn't necessarily have them, the more we need the fifth firefighter, and that's why this council is fighting for that. Are there specific engine companies that are statistically

overburdened relative to their current staffing based on call volume, run frequency, or simultaneous incident rates? And can you provide data to that— to the committee?
And those are the engine companies that historically in those 20 that we provide the fifth firefighter to, the ones that have heavier fire duty in those areas that have the bigger buildings.
Would you support a pilot program in the Bronx with a fifth firefighter in 20 of their busiest—
[interposing] We–,
20 of their busiest firehouses? Would you support that as an agency?
We would welcome— we would welcome additional resources.
Is that something that you're willing to fight with this council for with the Mamdani administration to fund?
We would welcome additional resources to deal with these— this fire problem that we have.

Rather than a binary choice between full citywide development and no deployment, has the FDNY evaluated a tiered or phased approach that prioritizes the highest-need companies first? And if you have, you know, how would you prioritize that? And the deployment of the fifth firefighter?

So the– those fires in the Bronx that we're seeing generally in six and seven story buildings, that are over 100 years old, old building stock, the potential for spread in those buildings is high. Some of these fires, the fire raced up through the stairway, so it's long hose line stretches. And you can compare that to Queens, that in some parts have smaller buildings, shorter hose line stretches, so that fifth firefighter would be much better off in areas with larger buildings, longer hose line stretches.
And does the fire department track instances where a company is committed to an active call and a second call comes in requiring a delayed or cross-district response?

That's something that we don't currently track. So we know, though, that in those areas, those busier areas with the companies that are doing– responding to more incidents, that there are times they're on one and then another company has to come over and respond to an incident because that original company is not available.
And when that other company comes over, doesn't that leave a gap in coverage for a large portion of that particular area that the second apparatus would–
[interposing] Our dispatchers–
would be covering?
in the communications office are able to manage and move resources around the city. So if they do see a gap in that coverage, then they'll move another company over as well.
So kind of someone is always without coverage. Like, if you keep moving them, somebody's always without coverage. If you keep moving—
[interposing] We continually assess and move resources around.
Yes. All right. At this point, I'd like to go over to my panel for questions on fifth firefighter.
Oh, your panel?
Yeah, well, we have anybody who's the next up.
Oh, okay. Yes, uh, sorry. Council Member–
[interposing] And if anybody wants to talk about fifth Firefighter and you already spoke, just please sign up for second round.
Got it. Council Member Wong followed by Council Member Palladino.

Okay, thank you, Chairs. I read the testimony here that the headcount is under budgeted by 190 people. My question is, how many of them are EMS positions, and what does the FY27 budget doing to close that gap?

So overall, the Department is under budgeted headcount, total agency, by 706 positions. 316 of that is on the

uniform side, driven by firefighters and lieutenants. 290 of that is EMS, and about 100 of that is civilian, largely because we just got positions added. So on the EMS side, unfortunately, because of the ongoing promotions to firefighter, although we are trying to staff up as much as possible and are aiming to hire large classes and continue to recruit folks to fill those vacancies, we do anticipate anticipate that it will take us quite some time to achieve budgeted headcount.

Okay, thank you. Regarding 600 ambulances in the field with 30 percent of them out of service, that is a very high number. Can you talk about what's being done? What's going on? You're waiting for parts? Is it a budget problem? That's 180 ambulances out of 600 that's out of service.

So the maximum amount of ambulances that we have in the field at any given time, and during the two tours that we run during the day is 340. So, that is distributed throughout the city. Although we have a fleet of 600, that's in case any ambulances, like the ones that are off

service, are off service, we can replace those ambulances with spares.

I see. Okay, thank you. My final question is on lithium-ion battery fires. I've never seen so many homes, five-alarm fires in homes, involving lithium batteries. How much funding is dedicated specifically to lithium battery enforcement, inspections, public education, and specialized firefighting equipment? Can you please talk about it?

There isn't really a separate funding pot tied to lithium-ion batteries. It's just something that's incorporated into everything. So when, say, our public safety— our fire safety education teams go out and do public education, this is one of the topics they cover. Similarly, on the fire prevention side, there are a number of staff that work on that. Chief Currao may have more to add.

Good afternoon, everybody. So as Commissioner Christoff had said, it's really a comprehensive approach. It's fire safety. It is tied to Local Law 40, working with other agencies to make

sure that, you know, that we don't have unregulated batteries that are being sold out there. It is addressing it as part of after– post-fire investigation. We work very, very closely with the Bureau of Fire Investigation. So it's a really comprehensive approach to be able to deal with that. And of course, the most important is education, right? And which has made a marked difference in I think raising the level of awareness that folks understand that they have to– it's really important to make sure that they have batteries that are UL-rated, that it's a complete system, the battery, the battery charger, not– you know, basic safety things, not charging it unattended, not charging it by means of egress. So it's really a holistic approach to get to the best safety outcome.
Do you think these vehicles should be stored indoors, or they– safer for them to be stored outside?
Are you talking– are you talking about electric vehicles?
Yes. Electric bikes or e-scooters, yes.

So we– what we do is we make sure for– in terms of electric vehicles, like cars, we don't regulate that. In terms of micromobility devices, what we do is make sure that they— the charging devices, the bike itself, the battery is up to the UL standards. We find that's the safest way to approach to, you know, to make sure that when that's in— those are implemented, those are charged, whether they're outside or inside of the battery charging cabinets, we make sure that they are at a very high level of safety standard.
Okay, thank you. Thank you.
Okay, great. Council Member Paladino followed by Restler.

Thank you very much. I want to go back if I could please, just for a moment, and then I'll move on. The fifth firefighter— I expected to see and hear a lot more enthusiasm about the fifth firefighter, because there was such an uproar when Bloomberg let that fifth fire— when that fifth firefighter were let go. I thought tonight— today I would hear a lot more enthusiasm.

And as the Chair asked about it, I seemed a very— I saw a very laid-back approach as to the importance of the fifth firefighter. I was rather— I was a little surprised by that.

So, thank you, Council Member. The fifth firefighter and the staffing is currently part of the UFA contract with the city that talks about the number and a medical leave level. But the— what we are trying to do, the priority in the Fire Department is we're trying to stabilize EMS. And the fifth firefighter is an important issue, but we're really focused more on stabilizing EMS, the staffing levels, the ambulance availability, the response times, making sure that we're able to fill our EMS recruit classes so that we can have ambulances arrive on scene in a timely manner.

Okay, good enough. Also, I'm going to circle back to a question I had asked a while back when we first started these hearings. I'm curious— I'm just one council member, and as for one council member, I've given close to $1 million of our money to the Fire Department. And that went for generators and other very important—

vehicles and such. I'm wondering, where is that money? And when is the Fire Department and EMS going to see the two vehicles that I did fund fully and the generators that I'm sure just not myself— like I said, I'm just one of 50. I'm sure other council members have done the same.
We can follow up on those specific projects and get back to you.

Oh, that's the third time I've heard that. It's okay. But please get back to me because it's a lot of money. And I— like I said, I'm one of 50, so I'm sure there's a lot of money floating out there in the millions of dollars that we need to know. Also, your budget, it says that, you know, we have achieved savings without harming our ability to carry out our mission of protecting life and property, and we strive to provide the best possible service to the people of New York. And you certainly, most certainly, have done that, and I thank you for all of that. I understand that we're all working under somewhat of a tight shoestring budget this year. I want to see— I

want to know how much of a shoestring budget is our FDNY, who should not be working with a shoestring budget at all, how much are they— how much is your budget so far for this year? Overall budget. Do you know?
